title: Three degrees (CCC 1554–1571)

segments.voice: Yesterday, what anointing does: strength, peace and courage for the sick. Your line was strength in sickness. Did you reach the person you thought of? Day one thousand one hundred five.

Sunday Mass in a parish church. A man in a white alb with a stole worn across one shoulder, like a sash, reads the Gospel and later sets the table at the altar. Another, with the stole hanging straight down around his neck, says the Eucharistic prayer. And once in a while, a third arrives with a tall pointed hat and a shepherd's staff, and it feels like an occasion. Three men, three roles at the same altar. A visitor might read it as three job titles on a company org chart. The Church tells it as one sacrament. Today's word is the shape of ordained ministry.
screen: `A SASH ACROSS ONE SHOULDER.` → `A STOLE HANGING STRAIGHT.` → `A MITER AND A STAFF.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says the sacrament of Holy Orders is one sacrament, given in three degrees: bishops, priests and deacons. One gift, held in three ways. The bishop comes first, and the Catechism calls his ordination the fullness of the sacrament. Catholic teaching sees bishops as successors of the apostles. A bishop teaches, sanctifies and governs a local church, and he alone ordains others. Next, priests. The Catechism calls them co-workers of the bishops. A priest can't do his ministry on his own authority: he works in communion with his bishop, and at his ordination he promises him respect and obedience. In the parish, the priest celebrates the Eucharist, hears confessions and anoints the sick. Then deacons. Here the Catechism makes a point worth hearing slowly: deacons are ordained not to the priesthood, but to service. In the Acts of the Apostles, the apostles ask the community to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to look after the daily distribution of food, so that the apostles can give themselves to prayer and the word. Catholic tradition links the deacon's office to that story. A deacon baptizes, proclaims the Gospel, preaches, assists at the altar, witnesses marriages, leads funerals, and gives himself to works of charity. The Catechism also notes that the Latin Church restored the deacon as a permanent ministry, one that can be given to married men. A letter of Ignatius of Antioch, which the Catechism quotes, holds the three together: he urges Christians to respect the deacons, the bishop and the presbyters, and says that without them there is no church. So the three aren't three separate jobs. They're one sacrament, held three ways, for serving one people.
screen: `ONE SACRAMENT, THREE DEGREES.` · `THE BISHOP: THE FULLNESS.` · `THE PRIEST: CO-WORKER WITH THE BISHOP.` · `THE DEACON: ORDAINED TO SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a deacon. Settle, and breathe. If you know a deacon, picture him: maybe a man who works a weekday job, then preaches on Sunday and visits the hospital on Tuesday night. If you don't know one, picture the person who serves in your community without being noticed: the one who stacks chairs, drives people to appointments, sits with the grieving. If you pray, you can ask God to sustain that person's service. If you don't, just hold them in gratitude for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Three degrees. One sacrament of Holy Orders, given to bishops, priests and deacons: the fullness, the co-workers, and those ordained to service. Today's word.
Your line: three orders. Today, find out the name of one deacon, priest or bishop who serves where you live, and say it once, kindly. Day one thousand one hundred five.

howItsDone: In the Catholic Church a bishop ordains bishops, priests and deacons by laying hands on them and saying the prayer of consecration; the three serve together in the diocese and the parish.

notes: CCC 1554–1571 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). 'Three degrees' and the bishop/priest/deacon summary follow CCC 1554, 1557, 1562–1567, 1569–1571.
Hook vestments: deacon's stole worn diagonally over the left shoulder; priest's stole hanging straight; bishop's miter and crozier. Confirm the description, and that a dalmatic is not needed.
'Only a bishop can ordain' (CCC 1576) is slightly outside the cited range; confirm.
Acts 6: 'Catholic tradition links the deacon's office to that story' is softened because Acts 6 does not use the noun 'deacon'; Keeper may adjust.
Myth reveal now says 'permanent deacons stay deacons for life' (no count claimed).
Ignatius (Trallians 3) paraphrased; Lightfoot's translation could be quoted if a Keeper confirms the wording. 'A very old letter' avoids a date.
Original διάκονος glossed as 'servant, minister' (standard lexicon meaning); confirm.

Editor: hook no longer says the stole is worn 'three ways' (a bishop's stole hangs like a priest's); 'not a ladder of importance' changed to 'one sacrament, held three ways', since the Church does speak of a hierarchy of degrees; 'a very old letter' replaced by 'which the Catechism quotes' (CCC 1554); myth reveal now acknowledges transitional deacons.
